LANGUAGE BORROWING: ETYMOLOGY AND CHANGES IN MEANING AND PRONUNCIATION OF ARABIC VOCABULARY IN SWAHILI. When speakers of two languages come into contact and interact, those languages can directly borrow from and influence each other phonologically, lexically, and grammatically. When the Arabs arrived on the East African coast, they encountered the Swahili, and it was then that Swahili borrowed words and sounds from Arabic that did not previously exist in the Swahili language. Secondly, Swahili also adopted some Arabic sounds and modified the way they are pronounced. This article investigates and identifies the etymology of certain Arabic words found in the Swahili language and examines how Arabic sounds were borrowed, altered, and adapted into Swahili. Furthermore, it explores how the original meanings of some words changed after being borrowed from Arabic. Theoretical frameworks and cognitive semantics of vocabulary were applied. Dr. Hamisi Babusa. Kenyatta University …………………………………………………………………………………………………….... Manuscript Info Abstract ……………………. …………………………………………………………………………………………………….... Introduction:- When Swahili came into contact with the Arabic language, it borrowed two things. It borrowed many Arabic words and adapted them, and secondly, it borrowed Arabic sounds that came with some of those words. The entry of Arabic words and sounds into the Swahili language resulted in two types of language change. The first type of change is the transformation or simplification of Arabic sounds so they can be pronounced by speakers of Swahili, which is a Bantu language. Secondly, there was a change in the original meaning of some Arabic words when they were incorporated into the Swahili language. This article will discuss language borrowing from Arabic into Swahili, the ways in which sound changes took place, and the alteration of the original meaning of some Arabic words borrowed into Swahili. This article employs two theories. The first is the structural theory, which deals with the changes in the sounds of words borrowed from the Arabic language. According to Mulder and Hervy (1975), this theory regards language as a large system comprised of many subsystems within it. They state that language is a system with five subsystems: semantics, pragmatics, syntax. Morphology and phonology. This article will focus on phonology, examining how sounds change. The second theory is that of cognitive lexical semantics. According to Paradis (2012), this theory deals with changes in meaning in words, which is one of the topics of this article. Hamisi Babusa. Address: Kenyatta University. Sound changes in borrowed Arabic words. Many Arabic words borrowed into the Swahili language, in addition to undergoing changes to adapt vowel patterns and conform to the structure of Swahili words, also experienced alterations to their original sounds. These sounds were changed because they did not exist at all in Swahili, and even if they had been borrowed directly, they would have caused pronunciation difficulties for Swahili speakers who were not accustomed to articulating these Arabic sounds. The following examples illustrate the changes in pronunciation of some Arabic words that have been incorporated into the Swahili language. Differentiation Between the Arabic ي (Yee) and the Swahili Vowel. The Arabic ي (Yee) or /y/ is the final consonant in the Arabic alphabet. There are some Arabic words that have a (yee) with a shadda. For example, MANIYYI منێ, NABIYYI نبێ, HAYYU حێ, TWAYYIB ﻄﯿﺐ, and MAYYITU مێټ. When these words were borrowed into Swahili, the ي (yee) was dropped and replaced by the vowel /i/. MANIYYI became MANII, NABIYYI became NABII. HAYYU became HAI, TWAYYIB became taib, MAYYITU became MAITI, etc.

Differentiation of the Arabic ع (‘Ain) and the Swahili Vowel

ﻉ (‘ain) is the eighteenth consonant in the Arabic alphabet. Some Arabic words that contain this sound include: ‘Aib عﯿﺐ, Mu‘allim معلم, ‘Ahdi عﻬد, ‘aqli عﻘل, and tis'a ﺗﺴعﺔ. When these words were borrowed and incorporated into Swahili, the Arabic ﻉ ‘ain, which is difficult for Africans to pronounce, was dropped and replaced with a vowel. For example, ‘aib became AIBU, mu’allim became MWALIMU, ‘ahdi became AHADI, ‘aqli became AKILI, and tis’a became TISA.

Change of ﻄ (Twee) in Arabic to /T/ in Swahili

Another sound change occurs where an Arabic word containing the ﻄ (twee) consonant is changed to /t/ after being borrowed into Swahili. For example, the following words are from Arabic: TWAYYIB ﻄﯿﺐ and TWAARIQ ﻄﺂﺮﻖ. When these words were borrowed and incorporated into the Swahili language, the ﻂ (twee) consonant was dropped and replaced with /t/, resulting in the Swahili words TARIKI and TAIB.

Change of ﺺ (Swaad) in Arabic to /S/ in Swahili

Arabic words that have the ﺺ (swaad) consonant, when entering the Swahili language, are changed so that ﺺ (swaad) becomes /s/. For example: SWAADIQ ﺻﺎدﻖ changed to SADIKI, SWAGHYR ﺻﻐﯿﺭ changed to SAGHIRI, and SWIRAAT ﺻﺮﺁﺖ changed to SIRATI.

Change of ﻖ (Qaaf) in Arabic to /K/ in Swahili

In the Arabic alphabet, there is ﻙ (kaaf) /k/ and ﻖ (qaaf). ﻖ (qaaf) is the twenty-first consonant in the Arabic alphabet, pronounced further back in the mouth than /k/, i.e., with contact at the soft palate and the back of the tongue. Bantu speakers did not have this sound, and when words with this Arabic sound were borrowed into Swahili, ﻖ (qaaf) was changed to /k/. For example: SWAADIQ ﺻﺎدﻖ became SADIKI, TWAARIQ ﻄﺂﺮﻖ became TARIKI, ‘AQLI عﻘل became AKILI, WARAQA ﻮﺭﻗﻪ became WARAKA, and WAQTI ﻮﻗﺖ became WAKATI.

Change of ﻇ (Dhwee) in Arabic to /Dh/ in Swahili

ﻇ (dhwee) is the seventeenth letter in the Arabic alphabet. When words containing this sound were borrowed and incorporated into Swahili, ﻇ (dhwee) was replaced by /dh/. For example: DHWAALIM ﺂلﻡﻇ became DHALIMU, and NADHWIIF نﻈﯿﻒ became NADHIFU.

Dropping of Arabic Vowels in Swahili

In some Arabic words, there is a prolonged sound or two vowels. When borrowed and incorporated into Swahili, one of the vowels is dropped, leaving only one. For example: TWAARIQ ﻄﺂﺮﻖ changed to become TARIKI, DHWAALIM ﻇﺂلﻡ changed to become DHALIMU, NADHWIIF نﻈﯿﻒ changed to become NADHIFU. Change of ﺽ ('Ddwad) from Arabic to /Dh/ in Swahili: ﺽ ('Ddwad) is the fifteenth consonant in the Arabic alphabet. Most experts classify this sound as /d/, but it is not /d/. It is a sound articulated with the front part of the tongue (not the tip) and the teeth. This sound poses a challenge to pronounce, especially for speakers who are not familiar with the Arabic language. The Swahili do not have this sound, so they looked for a similar one and found /dh/, and immediately words with ﺽ ('llwad) in Arabic changed and began to be pronounced with /dh/ after being incorporated into the Swahili language. An example is: AR'LLI ﺃﺮﺾ changes to become ARDHI; 'LLAR ABUROHD B n ﺮkn an k an ﺐﺮﺿDH. Change in /H/ That Is Voiced and /H/ That Is Unvoiced In the Arabic language, there are two types of /h/. The first is ﺡ /h/ unvoiced and is pronounced from the upper part of the throat. Then there is ﻫ /h/ that is voiced and is pronounced from the chest. In the Swahili language, there is only one /h/, which is pronounced in the throat. Those Arabic words containing the sound /h/ ﻫ that is voiced, when borrowed into the Swahili language, this sound is changed to an unvoiced /h/. for example: “AHDI عﻬد changed to become AHADI, JUHDI ﺠﻫد… The Dropping of Final Sounds in Arabic Words Some Arabic words have final sounds that are often used as suffixes at the end of the word and are usually ﺀ (hamza) and ﺓ /t/. for example: HAYAAI ﺤﻳﺎﺀ, the hamza is dropped and a vowel following /y/ is also removed, so the word changes to HAYA. SWADAQAATU ﺼدﻗﺎﺕ, the final /t/ is dropped and a vowel after /q/ is removed, /qaaf/ becomes /k/, and the word changes to SADAKA. RISAALATU ﺮﺴﺎلﺔ, the final /t/ is dropped and a vowel after /s/ is removed, so the word changes to RISALA. WARAQATU ﻮﺭﻗﺔ, the final /t/ is dropped and /qaaf/ becomes /k/, so the word changes to WARAKA. Transfer of Arabic Word Structures into Swahili: Swahili words are usually arranged in a CV-CV (consonant-vowel) structure. for example, KAKA, DADA, MAMA, etc. Most Arabic words, when borrowed, generally do not follow this pattern of the Swahili language. They usually have the structure CVCCV, etc. However, when they are borrowed and incorporated into Swahili, they are supplied with vowels and changed to follow the CV-CV structure. For example:
‘AHDI (CVCCV) عﻬد changed to become AHADI (VCVCV), JUHDI (CVCVCV) ﺠﻫد became JUHUDI (CVCVCVCV). However, there are some words that retained their Arabic structure when borrowed into Swahili, thereby introducing a new word structure into the Swahili language from Arabic. For example: AR’LLI ﺃﺮﺾ (VCCV) becomes ARDHI (VCCV), KHAMSIIN ﺨﻤﺴﯿﻦ (CVCVCCVC) — when this word was borrowed into Swahili, it retained its original Arabic structure, but underwent a few changes, namely, /kh/ changed to /h/, a vowel immediately after /s/ was dropped, and a vowel was added to the end of the word. But no vowel was inserted after /m/, so the Arabic structure was preserved as it entered Swahili and the word became HAMSINI (CVCVCVCV).

Changes in meaning for some of the borrowed Arabic words.
Most Arabic words borrowed and incorporated into Swahili retained their original meaning from Arabic. However, some words changed meaning after being borrowed and acquired new meanings in the Swahili language. This section will examine some words whose meanings changed following borrowing.

Dari is a Swahili word borrowed from Arabic ﺪﺍﺭ (dār). The original Arabic meaning of this word is HOUSE (NYUMBA), as seen in the phrase ﺪﺍﺭﺴﻼﻡ DĀR SALĀM meaning HOUSE OF PEACE. When borrowed into Swahili, however, its meaning changed—it no longer referred to a 'house' but rather to the upper part of a house, just below the roof.

Alhamisi is a Swahili word borrowed from the Arabic word ﺃﻠﺧﻤﻴﺱ (alkhamīs). According to the Arabic weekly calendar, Alkhamiis is the fifth day. But in Swahili, it is the sixth day of the week. Let us compare the days of the week in Arabic and Swahili:

Swahili               Arabic
Jumamosi (first day of the week)      ﻴﻮﻡﺍﻠﺴﺑﺖ (yaumu sabt)    the day of rest
Jumapili (second day of the week)     ﻳﻭﻢﺍﻷﺤﺪ (yaumul-ahad)  the first day of the week
Jumatatu (third day of the week)      ﻳﻭﻡﺍﻹﺜﻧﻴﻦ (yaumul-ithnayn)  the second day of the week
Jumanne (fourth day of the week)      ﻴﻭﻢﺍﻟﺜﻸﺘﺎﺀ (yaumu thulāthā')  the third day of the week
Jumatano (fifth day of the week)      ﺀﻭﻢﺍﻷﺮﺑﻌﺎﺀ (yaumul-arba'ā')   the fourth day of the week
Alhamisi (sixth day of the week)      ﺃﻠﺧﻤﻴﺱ (alkhamīs)      the fifth day of the week
Ijumaa (day of completing the week)   ﻴﻭﻢﺍﻟﺟﻤﻌﺔ (yaumul-jumu‘a)     the last day of the week

According to the comparison between Swahili and Arabic days, it is clear that the days do not align: the first day in Swahili (Jumamosi) in Arabic is the day of rest, and the second day in Swahili is the first day of the week in Arabic, and so forth. Swahili borrowed two words, ALHAMISI and IJUMAA, from Arabic. However, the word ALHAMISI—which meant ‘the fifth day’ in Arabic—when it entered the Swahili language, its meaning changed to ‘the sixth day of the week.’

Sakafu is a Swahili word borrowed from the Arabic ﺴﻘﻒ (saqf). In Arabic, saqf means CEILING, that is, the upper part of a house beneath the roof. However, when this word was borrowed into Swahili, its meaning changed to refer to the lower part of the house—that which is laid and cemented.

Nahau is another word borrowed from the Arabic ﺍﻟنﺤﻭ (an-nahwu), which originally means GRAMMAR in Arabic. However, when incorporated into Swahili, the word took on a new meaning: a group of words that together carry a special meaning not directly derived from the usual meanings of the individual words. Linguistics is a word that was also borrowed from the Arabic language ﺍﻹﺴﻡ (al-ismu), whose original meaning is NAME. When this word was borrowed and incorporated into Swahili, its meaning changed to refer to the discipline that studies and scientifically analyzes language. Waraka was also borrowed from the Arabic language ﻮﺭﻗﺔ (waraqatu). The original meaning of this word in Arabic is LEAF OF A TREE. However, when it was borrowed and incorporated into the Swahili language, its meaning changed to refer to documents written on a piece of paper that convey certain information. In conclusion, this article examines and analyzes the various phonological changes of Arabic words that were borrowed and incorporated into Swahili. After identifying various changes, it was determined that many Arabic words were adapted into Swahili after being borrowed, with their consonants altered to simplify pronunciation for Bantu speakers. In addition, there are sounds and pronunciation patterns that were borrowed directly from Arabic without any modification. Moreover, there were also changes in meaning in some of the borrowed Arabic words incorporated into the Swahili language. Therefore, the evidence shows that both changes in meaning and pronunciation occurred in some Swahili words borrowed from Arabic. References:- 1. Khamisi A. B. This article employs two theories. The first is the structural theory, which deals with the changes in the sounds of words borrowed from the Arabic language. According to Mulder and Hervy (1975), this theory regards language as a large system comprised of many subsystems within it. They state that language is a system with five subsystems: semantics, pragmatics, syntax.
Morphology and phonology. This article will focus on phonology, examining how sounds change.

discourses.source_txt: Sound changes in borrowed Arabic words. Many Arabic words borrowed into the Swahili language, in addition to undergoing changes to adapt vowel patterns and conform to the structure of Swahili words, also experienced alterations to their original sounds. These sounds were changed because they did not exist at all in Swahili, and even if they had been borrowed directly, they would have caused pronunciation difficulties for Swahili speakers who were not accustomed to articulating these Arabic sounds. The following examples illustrate the changes in pronunciation of some Arabic words that have been incorporated into the Swahili language.
discourses.translated_txt: Maneno ya Kiarabu yalibadilika kwa sababu ya kutopatikana kwa maneno ya Kiswahili, na hata kama yalipaswa kukopwa moja kwa moja, yangesababisha ugumu wa utamkaji kwa wasemaji wa Kiswahili ambao hawakuwa wamezoea kutaja sauti hizi za Kiarabu.

discourses.source_txt: For example, MANIYYI منێ, NABIYYI نبێ, HAYYU حێ, TWAYYIB ﻄﯿﺐ, and MAYYITU مێټ. When these words were borrowed into Swahili, the ي (yee) was dropped and replaced by the vowel /i/.

discourses.source_txt:
HAYYU became HAI, TWAYYIB became taib, MAYYITU became MAITI, etc.

Differentiation of the Arabic ع (‘Ain) and the Swahili Vowel

ﻉ (‘ain) is the eighteenth consonant in the Arabic alphabet. Some Arabic words that contain this sound include: ‘Aib عﯿﺐ, Mu‘allim معلم, ‘Ahdi عﻬد, ‘aqli عﻘل, and tis'a ﺗﺴعﺔ. When these words were borrowed and incorporated into Swahili, the Arabic ﻉ ‘ain, which is difficult for Africans to pronounce, was dropped and replaced with a vowel. For example, ‘aib became AIBU, mu’allim became MWALIMU, ‘ahdi became AHADI, ‘aqli became AKILI, and tis’a became TISA.

Change of ﻄ (Twee) in Arabic to /T/ in Swahili

Another sound change occurs where an Arabic word containing the ﻄ (twee) consonant is changed to /t/ after being borrowed into Swahili. For example, the following words are from Arabic: TWAYYIB ﻄﯿﺐ and TWAARIQ ﻄﺂﺮﻖ. When these words were borrowed and incorporated into the Swahili language, the ﻂ (twee) consonant was dropped and replaced with /t/, resulting in the Swahili words TARIKI and TAIB.

Change of ﺺ (Swaad) in Arabic to /S/ in Swahili

Arabic words that have the ﺺ (swaad) consonant, when entering the Swahili language, are changed so that ﺺ (swaad) becomes /s/. For example: SWAADIQ ﺻﺎدﻖ changed to SADIKI, SWAGHYR ﺻﻐﯿﺭ changed to SAGHIRI, and SWIRAAT ﺻﺮﺁﺖ changed to SIRATI.

Change of ﻖ (Qaaf) in Arabic to /K/ in Swahili

In the Arabic alphabet, there is ﻙ (kaaf) /k/ and ﻖ (qaaf). ﻖ (qaaf) is the twenty-first consonant in the Arabic alphabet, pronounced further back in the mouth than /k/, i.e., with contact at the soft palate and the back of the tongue. Bantu speakers did not have this sound, and when words with this Arabic sound were borrowed into Swahili, ﻖ (qaaf) was changed to /k/. For example: SWAADIQ ﺻﺎدﻖ became SADIKI, TWAARIQ ﻄﺂﺮﻖ became TARIKI, ‘AQLI عﻘل became AKILI, WARAQA ﻮﺭﻗﻪ became WARAKA, and WAQTI ﻮﻗﺖ became WAKATI.

Change of ﻇ (Dhwee) in Arabic to /Dh/ in Swahili

ﻇ (dhwee) is the seventeenth letter in the Arabic alphabet. When words containing this sound were borrowed and incorporated into Swahili, ﻇ (dhwee) was replaced by /dh/. For example: DHWAALIM ﺂلﻡﻇ became DHALIMU, and NADHWIIF نﻈﯿﻒ became NADHIFU.

Dropping of Arabic Vowels in Swahili

In some Arabic words, there is a prolonged sound or two vowels. When borrowed and incorporated into Swahili, one of the vowels is dropped, leaving only one.

‘AHDI (CVCCV) عﻬد changed to become AHADI (VCVCV), JUHDI (CVCVCV) ﺠﻫد became JUHUDI (CVCVCVCV). However, there are some words that retained their Arabic structure when borrowed into Swahili, thereby introducing a new word structure into the Swahili language from Arabic. For example: AR’LLI ﺃﺮﺾ (VCCV) becomes ARDHI (VCCV), KHAMSIIN ﺨﻤﺴﯿﻦ (CVCVCCVC) — when this word was borrowed into Swahili, it retained its original Arabic structure, but underwent a few changes, namely, /kh/ changed to /h/, a vowel immediately after /s/ was dropped, and a vowel was added to the end of the word. But no vowel was inserted after /m/, so the Arabic structure was preserved as it entered Swahili and the word became HAMSINI (CVCVCVCV).

Changes in meaning for some of the borrowed Arabic words.
Most Arabic words borrowed and incorporated into Swahili retained their original meaning from Arabic. However, some words changed meaning after being borrowed and acquired new meanings in the Swahili language. This section will examine some words whose meanings changed following borrowing.

Dari is a Swahili word borrowed from Arabic ﺪﺍﺭ (dār). The original Arabic meaning of this word is HOUSE (NYUMBA), as seen in the phrase ﺪﺍﺭﺴﻼﻡ DĀR SALĀM meaning HOUSE OF PEACE. When borrowed into Swahili, however, its meaning changed—it no longer referred to a 'house' but rather to the upper part of a house, just below the roof.

Alhamisi is a Swahili word borrowed from the Arabic word ﺃﻠﺧﻤﻴﺱ (alkhamīs). According to the Arabic weekly calendar, Alkhamiis is the fifth day. But in Swahili, it is the sixth day of the week. Let us compare the days of the week in Arabic and Swahili:

Swahili               Arabic
Jumamosi (first day of the week)      ﻴﻮﻡﺍﻠﺴﺑﺖ (yaumu sabt)    the day of rest
Jumapili (second day of the week)     ﻳﻭﻢﺍﻷﺤﺪ (yaumul-ahad)  the first day of the week
Jumatatu (third day of the week)      ﻳﻭﻡﺍﻹﺜﻧﻴﻦ (yaumul-ithnayn)  the second day of the week
Jumanne (fourth day of the week)      ﻴﻭﻢﺍﻟﺜﻸﺘﺎﺀ (yaumu thulāthā')  the third day of the week
Jumatano (fifth day of the week)      ﺀﻭﻢﺍﻷﺮﺑﻌﺎﺀ (yaumul-arba'ā')   the fourth day of the week
Alhamisi (sixth day of the week)      ﺃﻠﺧﻤﻴﺱ (alkhamīs)      the fifth day of the week
Ijumaa (day of completing the week)   ﻴﻭﻢﺍﻟﺟﻤﻌﺔ (yaumul-jumu‘a)     the last day of the week

According to the comparison between Swahili and Arabic days, it is clear that the days do not align: the first day in Swahili (Jumamosi) in Arabic is the day of rest, and the second day in Swahili is the first day of the week in Arabic, and so forth. Swahili borrowed two words, ALHAMISI and IJUMAA, from Arabic. However, the word ALHAMISI—which meant ‘the fifth day’ in Arabic—when it entered the Swahili language, its meaning changed to ‘the sixth day of the week.’

Sakafu is a Swahili word borrowed from the Arabic ﺴﻘﻒ (saqf). In Arabic, saqf means CEILING, that is, the upper part of a house beneath the roof. However, when this word was borrowed into Swahili, its meaning changed to refer to the lower part of the house—that which is laid and cemented.

Nahau is another word borrowed from the Arabic ﺍﻟنﺤﻭ (an-nahwu), which originally means GRAMMAR in Arabic. However, when incorporated into Swahili, the word took on a new meaning: a group of words that together carry a special meaning not directly derived from the usual meanings of the individual words.

In conclusion, this article examines and analyzes the various phonological changes of Arabic words that were borrowed and incorporated into Swahili.

discourses.source_txt: After identifying various changes, it was determined that many Arabic words were adapted into Swahili after being borrowed, with their consonants altered to simplify pronunciation for Bantu speakers. In addition, there are sounds and pronunciation patterns that were borrowed directly from Arabic without any modification. Moreover, there were also changes in meaning in some of the borrowed Arabic words incorporated into the Swahili language. Therefore, the evidence shows that both changes in meaning and pronunciation occurred in some Swahili words borrowed from Arabic.

Kwa kuongezea, kuna sauti na mifumo ya utamkaji ambayo ilipokopwa moja kwa moja kutoka Kiarabu bila marekebisho yoyote.
